predict.question: If you move a torch-free ball closer to a window light source, what happens to its shadow on the wall?

options.text: The shadow stays the same size

predict.why: Moving the object closer to the light spreads the blocked light over a wider area, making the shadow bigger.

experiment.title: Shadow stretching
steps: Stand near a sunlit window so light falls on a wall or a paper screen on the floor
Hold the ball close to the window and mark/observe the shadow size on the wall
Slowly move the ball away from the window towards the wall
Move the ball back close to the window again and compare
experiment.note: Do not look directly at the sun; use indirect sunlight through the window.

say: What happened to the shadow when the ball was near the window?
What happened when you moved it away?
Can you guess why that happens?
avoid: Don't say 'the shadow gets bigger because it's closer to light' before they notice it themselves

notice.question: What did you see about the shadow's size as the ball moved?
notice.lookFor: Child notices shadow is bigger when object is closer to light, smaller when farther away

hints.text: Watch the edges of the shadow on the wall, not just the ball
Compare shadow size when ball is near window vs far from window
Light spreads out from its source like a widening cone — think what happens when the object blocks it near versus far

reveal.explanation: Light travels in straight lines from its source. When an opaque object blocks these lines, a dark area called a shadow forms behind it. When the object is closer to the light, it blocks a wider spread of light rays, making the shadow larger. When it's farther from light (closer to the screen), it blocks a narrower set of rays, making the shadow smaller.
reveal.termMeaning: A shadow is formed when an opaque object blocks light travelling in straight lines, creating a dark region on the other side.

teachBack.prompt: Explain to a younger sibling why your shadow looks bigger when you stand close to a lamp and smaller when you stand far away.

revisits.question: Why do shadows at noon look shorter than in the evening?
revisits.answer: Because the sun's position changes the angle of light rays, changing shadow length

revisits.question: If you hold a book very close to a lamp, what happens to its shadow on the table?
revisits.answer: The shadow becomes larger because the book blocks more spreading light rays
